claim: Puttaswamy, Order of the Court (24 Aug 2017, signed by all nine judges): (i) M.P. Sharma is overruled on the view that privacy is not protected; (ii) Kharak Singh is overruled to the extent it says the same; (iii) privacy is protected as part of Article 21 and of the freedoms of Part III; (iv) later decisions saying so are correct.
source: K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India, 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges), Supreme Court official copy
page_or_section: Order of the Court, paras 1-2; PDF pp.546-547
note: Same as ledger POL03-D12; repeated in full because every part of this answer rests on it.

claim: Bench: M.P. Sharma (1954) was decided by eight judges and Kharak Singh (1962) by six; because the Attorney General argued both denied a right to privacy, a Constitution Bench on 18 Jul 2017 sent the issue to nine judges. The judgment of the Chief Justice and three others was delivered by Chandrachud J.; Chelameswar, Bobde, Sapre, Nariman and Kaul JJ. wrote separately.
source: K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India, 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges), Supreme Court official copy
page_or_section: Chandrachud J., Part A paras 2-5, PDF pp.5-7; Order para 1, p.546

claim: Puttaswamy conclusion 3(A)-(B): life and personal liberty are 'inalienable' and 'not creations of the Constitution'; the Constitution recognises them as inhering in each individual. So fundamental rights in Part III are protected, not granted, by the Constitution.
source: K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India, 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges), Supreme Court official copy
note: Chandrachud J. also writes that fundamental rights are 'primordial rights' preserved by the Constitution (Part G, PDF p.101).

claim: Puttaswamy conclusion 3(C), (D): privacy emerges primarily from Article 21, with elements from other Part III freedoms and dignity; the Court is not amending the Constitution but recognising a right already there.
value: privacy within Art 21 and Part III
source: K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India, 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges), Supreme Court official copy

claim: Puttaswamy conclusion 3(E)-(F): privacy is 'the constitutional core of human dignity'; it covers personal intimacies, family life, marriage, procreation, the home and sexual orientation; it is not lost merely because a person is in public.
source: K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India, 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges), Supreme Court official copy

claim: Puttaswamy conclusion 3(G): the Court did not list all entitlements within privacy; the Constitution 'must evolve with the felt necessities of time' and its meaning cannot be frozen as at adoption.
source: K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India, 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges), Supreme Court official copy

claim: Puttaswamy conclusion 3(H): privacy is not absolute; a restriction must pass legality, need (legitimate State aim) and proportionality, and the procedure under Article 21 must be fair, just and reasonable.
source: K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India, 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges), Supreme Court official copy

claim: Puttaswamy conclusion 3(I) and 5: privacy has a negative content (restrains State intrusion) and a positive content (State must take measures to protect it); informational privacy is a facet of privacy; threats come from State and non-State actors; the Court commended a robust data-protection regime to the Union.
value: negative and positive content; data protection
source: K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India, 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges), Supreme Court official copy
note: Ledger POL03-D15 covers conclusion 5; the Srikrishna Committee (OM of 31 Jul 2017) is named at Part S, PDF p.260.

claim: Puttaswamy, Chandrachud J.: the Gopalan idea that fundamental rights are separate 'silos' was replaced by the view that they overlap (Cooper and Maneka); ADM Jabalpur (1976) is 'seriously flawed' and does not survive; Kharak Singh's reliance on Gopalan was wrong.
value: overlap of rights; ADM Jabalpur overruled in terms
source: K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India, 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges), Supreme Court official copy
page_or_section: Part D; Part I, paras 119-121 (ADM Jabalpur, PDF pp.118-120; "must be and is accordingly overruled" p.120); Part T conclusion 2, p.261
note: Ledger POL03-D09 and D14 already cover the substance; use those ids first. [Audit 10 Nov 2026] Page corrected: the overruling words are on p.120.

claim: Puttaswamy, Chandrachud J., on the Section 377 case: the Koushal view that LGBT persons' rights were 'so-called' is unsustainable; their rights 'are real rights founded on sound constitutional doctrine'; sexual orientation is an essential attribute of privacy under Articles 14, 15 and 21.
source: K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India, 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges), Supreme Court official copy
note: Puttaswamy does not decide Section 377; it calls the Koushal reasoning flawed. The Court's later Navtej Johar ruling (2018) was not read for this note.

claim: Puttaswamy, Kaul J. (separate opinion): privacy protects the individual from interference by the State and non-State actors; 'privacy is one of the most important rights to be protected both against State and non-State actors'.
source: K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India, 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges), Supreme Court official copy
page_or_section: Kaul J., conclusion paras 77-79; PDF pp.539-540
note: Relevant to the scope of Fundamental Rights beyond the State (Art 12). [Audit 10 Nov 2026] Page corrected: quoted sentence runs across pp.539-540.

claim: Puttaswamy, Chandrachud J., para 84 quotes NALSA (2014): Article 21 protects 'one's personal autonomy, one's right to privacy', and transgender persons' 'values of privacy, self-identity, autonomy and personal integrity' are fundamental rights.
value: privacy, autonomy and identity as part of Arts 19 and 21
source: K.S. Puttaswamy v Union of India, 24 Aug 2017 (nine judges), Supreme Court official copy
note: Gives a concrete extension of Part III scope; the 2026 amendment to the Transgender Persons Act is researched under 2026-gs2-1.

claim: Article 21: 'No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law'; Maneka Gandhi (1978) read the procedure as having to be 'right and just and fair', which is the base the Puttaswamy test builds on.
source: Topic ledger POL-03
note: Cited from the topic ledger; not re-read.

claim: Also use ledger rows for: Article 12 'State' (POL03-A01), Article 13 (A03-A05), 'any person' versus 'citizen' rights (A10), the three-fold test (D13), data protection (D15) and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (POL03-X06).
source: Topic ledger POL-03

claim: Navtej Johar, Misra CJI (for himself and Khanwilkar J.), conclusions (ii), (vii), (xvi)-(xviii): Koushal's view that LGBT persons are a 'minuscule fraction' was 'constitutionally impermissible'; after Puttaswamy privacy is a fundamental right and discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation violates freedom of expression; s.377 IPC in its present form violates Article 19(1)(a), and so far as it penalises consensual sexual relations between two adults it 'cannot be regarded as constitutional'; Suresh Kumar Koushal was overruled.
value: Koushal overruled (6 Sep 2018) on the strength of Puttaswamy
source: Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India, WP(Crl) 76 of 2016, judgment 6 Sep 2018 (five judges), Supreme Court official copy
note: Read in the Court's own copy on 2026-11-10. The CJI's own conclusions rest s.377's invalidity on Art 19(1)(a) and on equality and dignity; other judges (Nariman, Chandrachud, Malhotra) wrote separately, and the 'Articles 21, 14 and 15' wording comes from the Delhi High Court (Naz Foundation) declaration quoted in the opinion, not the CJI's own list. Do not call this a 'new fundamental right': the Court applied Puttaswamy. [Audit 10 Nov 2026] Citation corrected: "after Puttaswamy privacy is a fundamental right" is conclusion (viii), not listed before. Conclusion (vii) is the freedom-of-expression point.

claim: Navtej Johar, Misra CJI, conclusions (i) and (vi): citing NALSA, identity has 'at the core' self-determination and cannot be 'pigeon-holed' to orientation; 'without the right to dignity, every other right would be rendered meaningless'; constitutional courts must protect every individual's dignity, including the right to express and choose 'without any impediments'.
source: Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India, WP(Crl) 76 of 2016, judgment 6 Sep 2018 (five judges), Supreme Court official copy
note: Quotes kept to phrases under 15 words. Read 2026-11-10 in the Court's own copy. Links to the NALSA row 2017-GS2-12-12 and to 2026-GS2-1 (self-identity). [Audit 10 Nov 2026] Page corrected: (i) on p.156; (vi) pp.159-160.

claim: Navtej Johar, Chandrachud J. (separate opinion): 'The judgment of four judges in Puttaswamy held that the right to sexual orientation is an intrinsic part of the right to privacy.' He treats this as the base for examining the Court's sexual-orientation cases.
source: Navtej Singh Johar v Union of India, WP(Crl) 76 of 2016, judgment 6 Sep 2018 (five judges), Supreme Court official copy
page_or_section: Chandrachud J., Part F opening (running head PART F); PDF p.332
note: Read 2026-11-10. The 'four judges' is Chandrachud J.'s own opinion in Puttaswamy (for himself and three others); the Order of the Court (claim -01) is the nine-judge ruling. [Audit 10 Nov 2026] Part corrected from E to F.

claim: Aadhaar judgment (26 Sep 2018), Sikri J. for the Chief Justice, himself and Khanwilkar J.: after privacy was declared a fundamental right in Puttaswamy, the Court applied a four-part proportionality test to the Aadhaar Act: a legitimate goal; suitability; no less restrictive equally effective alternative (necessity); no disproportionate impact on the right holder (balancing). It held the Act met that test.
value: proportionality four-stage test applied; Act upheld in main
source: K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India (Aadhaar), WP(C) 494 of 2012, judgment 26 Sep 2018, Supreme Court official copy
page_or_section: Summary and Conclusions, privacy answer (b) and proportionality item (e); PDF p.546 (triple test) and p.549 (four stages)
note: Read 2026-11-10 in the Court's own copy (Sikri J. for three; Chandrachud J. dissented separately; the dissent was not mined). The Court framed it as Puttaswamy's three-fold test (legality, need, proportionality) refined to four parts. Compare claim -07. [Audit 10 Nov 2026] Page corrected: four-part test is item (e) on p.549 (not 548); triple test p.546. PDF page numbers equal the printed "Page n of 567".

claim: Aadhaar judgment: privacy was balanced against dignity in the form of welfare. The majority said the petitioners claim 'dignity as a facet of right to privacy', while Section 7 offers subsidies and benefits to the marginalised, so both rights rest on human dignity; it held there was 'minimal intrusion' into privacy.
value: privacy and dignity weighed against welfare (s.7)
source: K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India (Aadhaar), WP(C) 494 of 2012, judgment 26 Sep 2018, Supreme Court official copy
page_or_section: Summary and Conclusions, privacy answer (c)-(j); PDF pp.547-551
note: Read 2026-11-10; paraphrase, with 'minimal intrusion' and the dignity phrase only. The conclusion section runs from PDF p.524. [Audit 10 Nov 2026] Page corrected: "minimal intrusion" is item (i) on p.550; dignity-v-welfare balance continues to p.551.

claim: Aadhaar judgment, operative limits that protect privacy: Regulation 27(1) allowing records to be kept five years was held bad in law (authentication records not beyond six months); Regulation 26's metabase 'impermissible'; s.33(1) read down to require a hearing; s.33(2) 'struck down'; and the part of s.57 letting a body corporate or individual seek authentication was held unconstitutional.
value: s.33(2) and part of s.57 struck; data-retention rule cut
source: K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v Union of India (Aadhaar), WP(C) 494 of 2012, judgment 26 Sep 2018, Supreme Court official copy
